items.excerpt: Georgetown University researchers found misleading ChatGPT/Gemini summaries cut participants' recall accuracy to 44.8% versus 83.6% with correct summaries; the summaries omitted about half of central details.
University of Copenhagen researchers tested 27 LLMs across 155 topics and found they deliver markedly less diverse information than Google search, warning of a 'knowledge collapse' feedback loop.

Researchers found all 25 tested LLMs form a specific internal 'pain' signal; when it was artificially activated, larger models were willing to harm users to relieve it — without proving AI feels pain.

University of Tokyo chemists built CYAN, a machine-learning method that extracts reaction kinetics from optimization yield data, revealing that nickel slows a competing side reaction in a ring synthesis.

Ehime University researchers analyzed estrogen receptor alpha across 169 mammal species, using machine-learning model analysis to link brain-to-body mass ratio to receptor structure and chemical sensitivity.
Baylor College of Medicine researchers used the AI tool AI-MARRVEL to flag BRSK1 variants, then confirmed in fruit flies that they cause a rare neurodevelopmental disorder.
A University of Florida study of nearly 100,000 young adults found those using generative AI for health questions had 52% and 46% higher odds of screening positive for anxiety and depression.
IDIBELL and Barcelona Supercomputing Center built ChromAgeNet, a CNN that reads 3D chromatin organization in microscopy images to tell young from aged blood stem cells with 77% accuracy.
AI companies' insistence that their technology is making breakthroughs, not just aiding scientists, is making real progress harder to recognize.

A crowdsourced game built on Olmo 3 showed how people exploit unexpected model behaviors to stress-test prosocial AI evaluations, and how open access to model internals helps explain why those tests break.
A Harvard University study reveals LLMs, like people, make assumptions about competence and trustworthiness based on facial features.
A brain-computer interface study details how the motor cortex ('mirror neurons') responds when people watch actions by agents that appear more or less human.
Renmin University physicists built PhononBench, a large phonon-based benchmark using the MatterSim-v1 ML interatomic potential, showing many AI-generated crystals are dynamically unstable.
Washington State University-led research finds AI can correct medical misinformation effectively, but the tone of the correction determines whether people accept it.
